item.title: MiBeeNvr: A Lightweight Home NVR System I Built
item.description:
I have several cameras at home — a few Xiaomi cameras, some DIY ESP32 cameras, and multiple Raspberry Pi CSI cameras. I’d been using cloud storage solutions, but I was never comfortable with them: vendor lock-in, network dependency, and the costs add up. So I decided to build my own NVR system, called MiBeeNvr.

Why Build MiBeeNvr

To be honest, I was never satisfied with existing cloud storage solutions. Take Xiaomi cameras, for example. By default, you can only view them through the Mi Home app. Recordings are either stored on an SD card (limited capacity, frequent plugging/unplugging) or in the cloud. Cloud storage costs tens of dollars per month, and there’s the privacy concern — you never know when the manufacturer might use your video data for AI training or sell it to third parties. Not to mention vendor lock-in — switching platforms is nearly impossible.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.3.1: Multi-Protocol Streaming and Native Xiaomi Camera Support
item.description:
#XQ|A lot of work went into the releases after v0.2.0. v0.3.x brings several major updates: native Xiaomi camera support, recording archiving, multi-protocol streaming architecture (WebRTC/HTTP-FLV/RTMP/SRT/LL-HLS), and a wave of security hardening. The architectural evolution from external dependencies to built-in implementation, from single protocol to full protocol support, was much more complex than I expected.

The previous post introduced v0.2.0’s 15 new features (v0.2.0 Update). If you haven’t read the first post, start with MiBeeNvr Introduction. v0.3.0 focuses on deep Xiaomi camera integration, and v0.3.1 builds on that with a complete multi-protocol streaming architecture. For the full changelog, see GitHub Release Notes.

item.title: ONVIF vs GB/T 28181: How They Work Inside — Plug-and-Play Devices vs System-Level Networking
item.description: After MiBeeNvr v0.9 shipped ONVIF auto-discovery, manual camera configuration was mostly gone. The next question was whether to add GB/T 28181 uplink support, so I dug through the mechanics of both protocols. Most comparison articles online stop at “ONVIF is the international standard, GB28181 is the Chinese national standard”—which carries zero information for someone writing code. This post breaks both protocols down to the signaling-flow and message level: how ONVIF discovers devices and obtains stream URIs; how GB28181’s 20-digit codes address everything, how INVITE negotiates a stream, and what PS encapsulation actually is.

item.title: The Surveillance Protocol Panorama: A Four-Layer Map from Access to Compliance — What Each Protocol Is and When to Use It
item.description: The previous post took ONVIF and GB/T 28181 apart down to signaling and messages. But building an NVR means the protocol environment extends well beyond those two: vendor-private APIs on the camera side, a view-library standard on the public-security side, Ministry-of-Transport standards for vehicles, WebRTC for browser viewing, HLS for public distribution, and a national-crypto compliance stack. This post lays out the entire landscape—each protocol gets four sections: what it is → key technical points → its relationship with other protocols → its value to an NVR. Beginners can read it as an index; veterans can jump straight to the priority table.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.12.0: Sub-streams, Adaptive Recording, and Full-path Observability
item.description:
MiBeeNvr v0.12.0 is out. This release goes after two everyday annoyances: watching the cameras on a phone, where a thumbnail-sized preview quietly pulls the full-resolution video underneath — eating data and heating the phone; and corridor or doorway cameras writing tens of GB a day that nobody ever replays.

Less disk

  • When nothing moves, the camera records less; the moment anything moves, it snaps back to full recording without dropping a frame. Quiet scenes measured at roughly 3/4 less disk
  • A louder sound, a doorbell, or a sensor signal also kicks it back to full recording
  • The replay timeline carries a green-to-red heat strip — the segments where something happened are visible at a glance
  • When the disk nears full, the quietest recordings are deleted first
  • Phone viewing defaults to a small, smooth stream: no stutter, no heat; one tap switches to HD for detail
  • When nobody is watching, that preview stream disconnects by itself — no camera connection or bandwidth tied up
